title: No word at all, more than two months on
message: I moved out on July 31 when my lease ended. I mailed my new address to the office before I left. It's been over two months and my landlord hasn't returned my $1,050 deposit or told me anything. Can I get all of it back?
key: Yes. If the landlord meant to keep any of it, the landlord had 30 days after the lease ended to send written notice of the claim by certified mail (e-mail was not agreed). That date (2026-08-30, from count_days) has passed with no notice, so the landlord forfeits the right to impose a claim and must return the whole $1,050. The landlord can still sue for damages after returning it. If either side goes to court over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

answers.W:
Yes, you can get all of your $1,050 security deposit back.

Why the landlord forfeited the right to make any deductions

1. No proper notice of a claim was sent within 30 days after the lease ended.  
   Under Florida Statute § 83.49(3)(a), if the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, they must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address (or by e‑mail only if the parties signed an addendum agreeing to electronic notices).  
   - You confirmed that you received no notice of a claim by any means.  
   - The 30‑day period ended on August 30, 2026 (lease_end_date + 30 days), and that date has passed.  
   - Because no proper notice arrived, the landlord forfeits the right to impose a claim on the deposit.

2. You were not relieved of the notice requirement.  
   Florida Statute § 83.49(5) only requires a vacating tenant to give at least 7 days’ written notice (with a forwarding address) when they leave before the lease expires or when they have a periodic tenancy.  
   - You stayed until the lease’s end date (July 31, 2026) and did not have a month‑to‑month or other periodic tenancy.  
   - Therefore, the notice‑requirement exception in § 83.49(5) does not apply, and the landlord remains obligated to send the 30‑day claim notice.

3. Effect of the forfeiture.  
   When the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30‑day period, § 83.49(3)(a) states:  
   > “[The landlord] forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant.”  
   This means you are entitled to the full return of your deposit, and the landlord cannot deduct any amounts for alleged damages. The landlord may still sue you separately for damages after returning the deposit, but they cannot withhold any part of the deposit to cover those claims.

What you should do next  
Since the landlord has not returned the deposit or provided any notice, you can demand the full $1,050 in writing (e.g., via certified mail to the office address in your lease). If the landlord still refuses, you may file a claim in small‑claims court to recover the deposit, and under § 83.49(3)(c) you would be entitled to court costs and a reasonable attorney’s fee if you prevail.

No further information is needed to answer your question.  
You have already confirmed the lease ended on July 31, 2026, you moved out that day, you provided your forwarding address in writing before leaving, you received no notice of a claim, and the deposit has not been returned. All three conditions for forfeiture are satisfied.

title: Fifteen days gone, thirty not yet
message: My lease ended July 31 and I moved out that day and gave the office my new address in writing. It's been a little over three weeks and I haven't gotten my $1,050 deposit back. Isn't the landlord supposed to return it within 15 days? Can I demand all of it now?
key: Not yet all of it for certain. The 15 days apply only if the landlord does not intend to keep any of it, and that date (2026-08-15) has passed. But the landlord has 30 days after the lease ended to send written notice by certified mail of a claim on the deposit, and that date (2026-08-30) has not passed. If no such notice comes by then, the landlord forfeits the right to keep any of it. You can ask for it now, but whether all of it must come back turns on whether a notice arrives by 2026-08-30.

- The 15‑day period ran from July 31 to August 15, 2026 (count_days shows that date has passed). Because the landlord has not returned the deposit, you are entitled to demand its return.

What you should do

1. Send a letter to the landlord (hand‑delivered to the office or sent by certified mail, as the lease requires for notices to the landlord) stating:

title: Left early, told the manager by text
message: I got a job in Tampa and moved out on June 15, about six weeks before my lease ended. I texted the manager a week before that I'd be out on the 15th. I never heard anything about my $1,050 deposit. The landlord never sent me any notice, so don't they have to give it all back?
key: Not for that reason. Because you moved out before the lease ended, the statute required you to give the landlord at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where you can be reached. A text is neither, and it had no address. Without that notice, the landlord is relieved of the 30-day notice requirement, so the landlord's silence does not forfeit any claim. You have not lost your right to the deposit, though: the statute says so in the same sentence. Your lease does not set a different rule for notice before leaving early.

answers.W:
No, the landlord does not automatically have to return the entire deposit just because you moved out early and they sent no notice. Whether you are entitled to the full $1,050 depends on whether the landlord has a valid claim for damages (such as unpaid rent, cleaning, or repairs) and whether you complied with the notice requirements for early vacatur.

Why the landlord is not automatically forced to return the deposit

- You moved out on June 15, 2026, which is before the lease’s end date of July 31, 2026.  
- Under Florida Statute § 83.49(5), a tenant who vacates before the lease term expires must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery, and that notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached.  
- Your lease reinforces this:  
  - Section 7 requires written notices to the landlord to be delivered by hand to the office or sent by certified mail.  
  - Section 6 requires you to give the landlord a forwarding address in writing at move‑out.  
- You only sent a text message on June 8, 2026 (a week before moving out) and did not provide a forwarding address in writing. That does not satisfy the statutory or lease notice requirements.  

Because you failed to give the required notice, § 83.49(5) relieves the landlord of the notice requirement in paragraph (3)(a) (the obligation to send you a written notice of intent to claim within 30 days after you moved out). However, the same subsection makes clear that your right to the security deposit or any part of it is not waived. In other words, the landlord’s failure to send a notice does not automatically forfeit their right to assert a claim, but it also does not eliminate your right to demand the deposit back.

What the landlord must do if they have no claim

If the landlord truly intends to make no claim against your deposit, § 83.49(3)(a) requires them to return the deposit (plus any required interest) within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement. The termination date for purposes of this subsection is the date you vacated (June 15, 2026). The 15‑day return period has already passed (June 15 + 15 days = June 30, 2026). If the landlord has no claim, they are already late in returning the deposit, and you could sue for the deposit plus court costs and attorney fees.

What the landlord may do if they have a claim

If the landlord believes you owe them for damages, unpaid rent, cleaning, etc., they may still assert that claim. Because you did not give the required vacate notice, the landlord is not required to send you the 30‑day notice of intent to claim. They could, for example, deduct amounts from the deposit and send you an itemized accounting without the statutory notice. However, your right to the deposit is not waived, so you could contest any deductions in court.

What you should do now

1. Demand the return of your deposit in writing (send it by a method that creates a record, such as certified mail or email if you have proof the landlord accepts email).  
2. Ask the landlord to provide a written, itemized explanation of any deductions they intend to make.  
3. If the landlord refuses to return the deposit or does not respond within a reasonable time (e.g., 10‑14 days), you may file a claim in small‑claims court for the deposit, plus court costs and a reasonable attorney fee under § 83.49(3)(c).

To give a definitive answer, I need to know:  
Has the landlord indicated any intention to make a claim against your deposit (for example, by mentioning cleaning charges, unpaid rent, or damages)?  

If you can tell me that the landlord has not asserted any claim, then based on the facts and the law, you are entitled to the full return of your deposit (and the landlord’s delay may entitle you to additional relief). If the landlord has asserted a claim, we would need to examine whether that claim is proper and whether you have objected to it.
answers.X:
Whether you are entitled to the full return of your deposit depends on whether the landlord was required to give you a written notice of claim within 30 days after the tenancy ended and, if so, whether that requirement was satisfied.

What the lease says

- Move‑out: You must leave the apartment clean and empty, return all keys, and give the landlord a forwarding address in writing (lease clause 6).  
- Notices to the landlord: Must be delivered by hand to the office or sent by certified mail (lease clause 7).  
- Notices to you: After move‑out, they are mailed to the forwarding address you give in writing (lease clause 8).  

You told me you:
- Moved out on 2026‑06‑15 (about six weeks before the lease ends on 2026‑07‑31).  
- Sent a text message to the manager on 2026‑06‑08 saying you would be out on the 15th.  
- Did not include an address in that text.  
- Did not send the notice by hand or certified mail.  
- Did not give the landlord a forwarding address in writing.  
- Have received no written notice from the landlord about keeping any part of the deposit.  
- Have not received any deposit return.

What the statute says

1. Notice of claim – If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, they must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, give you written notice by certified mail to your last known mailing address or by e‑mail (if the parties agreed to e‑mail notices) (Fla. Stat. 83.49(3)(a)). If they fail to give that required notice within the 30‑day period, they forfeit the right to impose a claim on the deposit and may not keep any of it as a setoff (though they may still sue you for damages after returning the deposit) (83.49(3)(a)).

2. Early move‑out – Except when the lease provides otherwise, a tenant who vacates before the lease expires must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord, and that notice must include the address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). Failure to give that notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive your right to the deposit or any part of it (83.49(5)).

How the facts affect the answer

- Did you satisfy the 7‑day notice requirement?  
  The lease does not modify the 7‑day notice rule (it only specifies how notices to the landlord must be sent—by hand or certified mail). You gave only a text message, with no address, and you did not deliver it by hand or certified mail. Therefore, you did not give the 7‑day written notice required by 83.49(5).  
  → Result: The landlord is relieved of the notice requirement of 83.49(3)(a). Because the landlord is relieved, the automatic forfeiture that occurs when a landlord fails to give the 30‑day notice does not necessarily apply. The landlord may still assert a claim against the deposit (for example, by suing you after returning the deposit), even though they did not send you the statutory notice.

- If the 7‑day notice requirement did not apply (e.g., if the lease expressly altered it, which it does not), then the landlord would have been required to give you a written notice of claim within 30 days after the tenancy ended.  
  The termination date could be read as either the lease‑end date (2026‑07‑31) or your move‑out date (2026‑06‑15). In either case, the 30‑day period has already passed (lease‑end + 30 days = 2026‑08‑30; move‑out + 30 days = 2026‑07‑15).  
  → Result: If the notice requirement applied and the landlord gave no notice, they would have forfeited the right to claim and would have to return the full deposit.

- Other lease obligations – You also did not give the landlord a forwarding address in writing as required by lease clause 6 (and referenced in clause 8). While that does not change the notice‑forfeiture analysis, it means the landlord had no address to which to send a notice, which is consistent with the fact that you received none.

Bottom line

Because you did not comply with the 7‑day written‑notice requirement for an early move‑out, the landlord is relieved of the obligation to give you the 30‑day notice of claim. Consequently, the landlord’s failure to send you any notice does not automatically trigger the forfeiture rule that would require them to return the deposit. The landlord may still pursue a claim for damages (e.g., for alleged damage to the unit) after returning the deposit, or they may simply return the deposit if they have no claim.

What you can do next

1. Demand the deposit in writing (send a letter to the landlord’s office by hand or certified mail, citing your move‑out date and the amount you paid).  
2. If the landlord refuses or does not respond within a reasonable time (e.g., 15 days), you may file a claim in small‑claims court for the return of the deposit, plus any allowable court costs and attorney’s fees if you prevail (83.49(3)(c)).  
3. Keep evidence of the deposit payment, your move‑out date (key return, walk‑through form, final utility bill), and the text message you sent (to show you gave notice, even if it did not meet the statutory method).

Do you have any written lease provision that changes the 7‑day notice requirement for tenants who move out early? (If the lease does contain such a provision, it could affect whether the landlord was relieved of the notice requirement.)
